newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE- Amputees by-product of Sri Lanka war.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE- Amputees by-product of Sri Lanka war.

text.p: Sergeant Athula Chandrasiri of the Sri Lankan army wanted a drink of water while on patrol at Velvettithurai, in the former northern Jaffna stronghold of separatist Tamil Tiger guerrillas.
But the 33-year-old soldier would never make it to a nearby well. A sudden explosion brought him down.

"However much I tried, I couldn't stand up. Then, to my horror, I realised my left leg was missing," he told Reuters at Ranaviru Sevana, an army rehabilitation centre for disabled soldiers in a Colombo suburb.

An anti-personnel mine, apparently planted by Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) guerrillas before they fled Jaffna ahead of advancing soldiers, exploded when Chandrasiri stepped on it, shredding his leg up to the thigh.
About six months after the accident, Chandrasiri was equipped with an artificial limb and was ready to join a long queue of disabled soldiers facing an uncertain future.
"It took me a long time to realise that life can go on without one leg. I still have to find out how life will treat me as a war victim," he said.
The LTTE are waging a war for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in predominantly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war, but doctors say they probably were the lucky ones. CIVILIANS ARE VICTIMS, TOO
Sixteen-year-old Dorothy Calistus is also a victim of Sri Lanka's ethnic war, now in its 14th year.

Dorothy says an air force plane bombed her village near Kilinochchi in the rebels' northern heartland one morning in September 1996. Her mother died instantly and she lost a leg after being hit by a shrapnel.
At least two people died and 15 of her neighbours were wounded in the bombing, Dorothy says.

"I want to go back to my village and go back to school. And I have a little sister to look after," Dorothy told Reuters at the Colombo Friend in Need Society, where she had been sent by doctors to be fitted with an artificial leg.
"Long after the war is over, these people will be suffering. It is a problem of the future," said Gamini Goonetilleke, a surgeon who specialises in treating amputees.
Goonetilleke said one area Sri Lanka needs to seriously concentrate on is caring for amputees, whose numbers have been steadily rising since the separatist war began in 1983.
At least 3,000 soldiers have been permanently disabled by the war, most of them victims of mines, Goonetilleke said.
"The number of LTTE rebels and civilians living in the north and east who have been disabled is not known, but undoubtedly their numbers are very high," he said.
As it is with the army, and probably with the rebels, most amputees are in the 18-30 age group, felled in the prime of their lives, said Brigadier Dudley Perera, director of army rehabilitation.
"What the enemy wants is to make soldiers disabled soldiers. Then the liability to the state is more," Perera said.
"Even if the war ends, these people will suffer. And the state has to look after them," he added.

At least for soldiers, the army has created a rehabilitation programme, which begins with treating war wounds and ends with vocational training that enables victims to take suitable jobs. LOSING A LIMB IS A PERMANENT SCAR
But for many soldiers, returning to civilian life with an arm or leg missing is a painful experience.

"They feel useless without a limb. In many instances their girlfriends have left them. Also, our society in general is not tolerant of the disabled. It takes a lot of determination on the part of the victim to overcome these problems," Goonetilleke said.
Soldiers are entitled to free artificial limbs and unlimited physiotherapy sessions that enable them to bounce back at least physically.
Sri Lanka now uses Indian technology to successfully manufacture the Jaipur Foot, a low cost prosthesis developed by an Indian doctor in the 1970s.
"We can produce a Jaipur limb for 3,500 rupees ($60) whereas an imported limb would cost more than 20,000 rupees," said Rupa Jayasekera, secretary of the Colombo Friend in Need Society.
Since it began producing the limbs in 1985, the society has given out about 7,500 of them, more than 5,000 going to victims of war, she said.
